newsitem.title: CANADA: Mobil exec rails against U.S. sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Mobil exec rails against U.S. sanctions.

text.p: A senior Mobil Corp executive on Wednesday railed against U.S. sanctions policy, saying the unilaterial approach displayed "proposterous arrogance" on the part of the administration.

Mobil, a long-time critic of unilateral U.S. policies, is particularly worried about renewed threats of new sanctions being placed on Nigeria, where the Fairfax, Virginia-based oil major is the second-largest foreign operator.

"This is just proposterous arrogance on the part of the U.S. government thinking that they could impose their will, their values on the rest of the world on a timeframe that suits the American politician," said Mobil Executive Vice-President Paul Hoenmans.

Mobil Corp has been locked out of lucrative oil production deals in Libya, Iran, Iraq and other countries now blacklisted by the United States, leaving the way open for oil majors from other countries to grab concessions.

"We've been active in all those countries before sanctions were placed on these countries and we'd love to go back to each one of them again," Hoenmans said at Mobil's Canadian headquarters on Wednesday.

The threat of sanctions against Nigeria has intensified since late 1995 when the country's military government hanged writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight associates of the Movement for the Survival of Ogoni Peoples.
The U.S. State Department spokesman on Wednesday referred to the administration's "difficult relationship with Nigeria."

Hoenmans said Mobil, which has operated in the west African nation for about three decades, does not support the government, which was not democratically elected and has a poor record on human rights.

"On the other hand, that is the government of the land and they are working in their land in a way that their population, at least up until now, tolerates and in many cases supports," said Mobil's Canadian-born No. 2 executive, who retires in August.
The company favored generating wealth within the country as a long-term solution to civil strife, rather than making economic conditions worse through sanctions, he said.

He also said U.S. sanctions in general were making it difficult for American oil companies to operate and find partners in other countries, citing figures that said about 72 percent of the world's population were under some form of U.S. sanction.

"A good part of the world that the upstream industry depends on for one reason or another is sanction territory for the United States at this time," Hoenmans said. ((Jeffrey Jones, Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
